summaries.example: Imagine a family of dogs living in different places. Over many generations, their bodies might become somewhat different because of their surroundings. Buffon used ideas like this to discuss how related animals could develop different forms. But he also used a test: if two kinds of animals could not produce fertile young together, he treated them as different species.
summaries.summary: This entry explains how people thought about changing living things before Darwin’s Origin of Species. The word “evolution” once usually meant the development of one individual embryo. The entry therefore often uses “transformism” for older ideas about species changing through history. Ancient atomists imagined life forms arising through natural processes, while Platonic, Stoic, and many Christian, Jewish, and Islamic traditions emphasized order, purpose, or creation. Aristotle explained living development through an inner organizing principle and helped support ideas of species lasting through generations. Later thinkers debated Earth’s history, fossils, reproduction, and whether matter could organize itself. In the eighteenth century, Buffon connected natural history with reproduction, geography, and changing environments. In the nineteenth century, Lamarck offered a systematic transformist theory, while Cuvier defended separate major body plans and extinction. These debates created an important background for Darwin, even though they were not Darwin’s theory.
key_ideas: People discussed the possibility of changing species long before Darwin.
Some ancient thinkers imagined life arising through natural, chance-like processes.
Other thinkers argued that living things showed purpose or design.
Aristotle and many later thinkers supported lasting forms, although local changes could happen.
In the 1700s and 1800s, new ideas about fossils, embryos, matter, and Earth’s history encouraged more discussion of species change.
Lamarck developed an early organized theory that species changed over time, while Cuvier argued that major kinds of animals had separate body plans and that some species had become extinct.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history shows that scientific ideas usually grow from many earlier questions. Before Darwin, people were already asking whether species were permanent, how embryos develop, what fossils reveal, and whether nature has its own powers. Studying these debates also teaches us not to place modern meanings onto old words too quickly. “Evolution,” “species,” and “design” did not always mean exactly what they mean today.

important_terms.definition: The idea that living kinds can change across long periods of history.
A group understood as connected through reproduction across generations.
The belief that a living kind stays essentially the same over time.
The study of how living things begin and develop, especially before birth or hatching.

questions_to_think_about: Why might people disagree about whether a kind of animal can change into another kind?
What evidence could help us decide whether two groups belong to one species?
Can a living thing have both a stable pattern and small changes?
Why would fossils matter when people study the history of life?

summaries.example: Consider the horse and the donkey. Buffon noted their anatomical resemblance, which could suggest a shared historical origin, but he also used hybrid infertility to argue that they were distinct species. He treated a species not mainly as a class defined by visible features, but as a continuing reproductive lineage. Later, his account of environmental “degeneration” allowed historical differences within lineages, although Buffon did not develop a full transformist theory in the Lamarckian sense.
summaries.summary: Evolutionary Thought Before Darwin surveys theories about the history of living forms from antiquity through the decades before 1859. It begins with a terminological warning: before the nineteenth century, “evolution” usually referred to embryological development, so the entry generally calls pre-Darwinian theories of species change “transformism.” Ancient atomists, especially through Lucretius, offered a naturalistic account in which forms emerged through undirected processes and unsuitable forms disappeared. Platonic, Stoic, and related traditions opposed this with arguments from rational order and design. Aristotle replaced an external designer’s role with an internal teleological principle in organisms, while his account of generation supported continuity of species forms; medieval authors revised these ideas within Augustinian and other theological settings without producing one uniform doctrine of essentialism. Early modern mechanism and pre-existence theories linked embryology to species fixity, but empirical problems eventually encouraged dynamic accounts of matter and epigenetic development. Maupertuis and Buffon connected generation, inheritance, environment, and historical change. Buffon’s species concept emphasized reproductive continuity and material succession, while his later “degeneration” allowed substantial lineage differences. In the early nineteenth century, Lamarck formulated a systematic transformism, Geoffroy defended unity of anatomical type, and Cuvier argued for autonomous body plans and extinction. British debates then included critiques by Lyell, developmental and archetypal theories associated with Owen, popular transformism in Chambers, and Spencer’s development hypothesis. key_ideas: The entry distinguishes older theories of species change from the later Darwinian use of “evolution,” and uses “transformism” for much of the pre-Darwinian discussion.
Ancient atomists proposed naturalistic, chance-like origins, while Platonic, Stoic, Aristotelian, and related traditions developed influential arguments for order, purpose, or enduring forms.

Aristotle’s biological account differs from a simple claim that species are rigid essences: he explained generation through an internal organizing principle, and medieval thinkers combined his ideas with theories of creation in varied ways.

Seventeenth-century mechanism and pre-existence theories moved the origin of organisms and species back to an initial creation, strengthening species fixity but creating difficulties for variation, hybrids, regeneration, and fossils.

Buffon redefined a species as a materially connected succession of ancestors and descendants, used reproductive fertility as an important criterion, and later allowed extensive environmental differentiation without fully endorsing transformism.

Lamarck proposed a coherent theory of historical change driven by active matter, with local adaptation and inherited acquired characters as a diversifying process; Cuvier opposed transformism through comparative anatomy, distinct body plans, and evidence for extinction.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history clarifies that Darwin entered an already crowded field of arguments about form, function, fossils, reproduction, inheritance, Earth history, and the powers of matter. It also shows why “evolution before Darwin” should not be reduced to a simple march toward natural selection. Earlier thinkers proposed different mechanisms and different pictures of historical order: chance-like formation, divine creation, internal teleology, degeneration, progressive development, archetypal laws, or local adaptation. Understanding those distinctions helps explain both Darwin’s originality and the intellectual problems his theory inherited.

important_terms.definition: A historical theory that species change over time; the term was widely used in French biological discussions before “evolution” took its later meaning.
A philosophical or biological account in which living forms have purposes or organized ends; ancient versions could appeal to an external designer, while Aristotle emphasized an internal principle.
The view that a species or its essential form remains stable through historical time.
A theory that organisms, or their earliest germs, already existed from the first creation and later developed rather than originating anew.
A theory of development in which the organism becomes organized over time rather than merely unfolding from a fully formed miniature.
Buffon’s account of an organizing material principle that shapes organic matter during generation and helps preserve a lineage.
A resemblance based on corresponding structural parts, even when those parts serve different functions.
A resemblance based chiefly on similar function or adaptation, rather than on corresponding underlying parts.

questions_to_think_about: What is gained, and what is lost, when a species is defined by reproductive continuity rather than by shared visible traits?
How did theories of embryological development influence theories about the historical origin of species?
Why could the same evidence—such as anatomical similarity—support different conclusions for Buffon, Geoffroy, or Cuvier?
How does Cuvier’s distinction among body plans challenge a simple ladder from simpler to more complex life?
Why is it historically misleading to treat every earlier theory of species change as an early version of Darwin’s natural selection?

summaries.example: Suppose two kinds of rabbits look different because one group lives in a cold region and another in a warm region. One thinker might say they are still one species if they can mate and have fertile young. Another might focus on their body shapes and classify them separately. Buffon’s approach gave special importance to reproductive connection, while other naturalists relied more on visible structure or classification. Their disagreement was partly about what a species really is.
summaries.summary: This entry follows ideas about species change from ancient Greece and Rome to the period immediately before Darwin. It explains that the word “evolution” once mainly meant the development of an individual embryo, so the older theory of species changing through history is usually called transformism. Ancient atomists, later represented by Lucretius, imagined living forms arising through natural processes that included chance-like sorting. Plato, Stoics, and related traditions argued instead that the order and complexity of living things pointed to purpose or rational organization. Aristotle offered a different kind of purpose: living beings develop through an internal organizing principle, and species continue through generation. Medieval philosophers and theologians revised these ideas in discussions of creation, time, and the possibility of new species, so their views were more varied than a simple “fixed species” story suggests. In the seventeenth century, mechanical philosophy and pre-existence theories connected species permanence to the idea that organisms or germs were present from the world’s beginning. Problems involving hybrids, variation, fossils, and development encouraged new theories of active matter and epigenesis. Maupertuis and Buffon helped connect embryology with inheritance and environmental change. Buffon allowed historical differences within connected lineages but did not become a full transformist. In the nineteenth century, Lamarck developed a systematic theory of species change, while Geoffroy emphasized unity of anatomical type and Cuvier defended separate body plans and extinction. key_ideas: Long before Darwin, philosophers and naturalists debated whether living kinds were fixed or could change.
Ancient atomists described natural origins involving chance-like processes, while Plato and later traditions argued that order and complex structure required more than chance.
Aristotle’s biology emphasized an inner organizing principle in living things. Medieval thinkers combined Aristotelian ideas with theories of divine creation in several different ways.
Early modern pre-existence theories said organisms or their germs were present from the beginning. This helped explain organized development but made species change difficult to accept.

Buffon studied reproduction, anatomy, geography, and changing environments. He defined species through continuing reproductive relationships and later described environmentally produced “degenerations.”
Lamarck argued for an ascending history of life and a role for inherited acquired traits. Cuvier disagreed, using comparative anatomy, separate body plans, and fossils showing extinction.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because it reveals that the question “Did species change?” was tied to many other questions: What is a species? How does an embryo form? Can matter be active? What do fossils tell us? Does nature have purposes? Different answers produced different theories of life’s history. Learning this background helps us understand why Darwin’s theory was both a major change and a response to problems that earlier thinkers had already explored.

important_terms.definition: The idea that species can change over many generations; older writers often used this idea before “evolution” had its modern meaning.
A living kind considered either as a classification group or as a continuing line of organisms connected by reproduction.
The belief that a species keeps its basic nature over time, even if individuals vary in less important features.
The study of how an individual organism forms and develops before birth or hatching.
The view that living things have purposes or organized functions. Some versions point to a designer; Aristotle’s version emphasized an internal cause.
The idea that a tiny organism, or its first seed, was already present from the beginning and later unfolded.
A planned arrangement of animal structures shared by a broad group, such as one of Cuvier’s major body plans.
The claim that a species or group changes into another through historical time.

questions_to_think_about: If two animals look different but can produce fertile offspring, should we call them one species? Why?
Why might a theory about how an embryo develops affect a theory about how species originate?
What would fossils show if species really changed gradually? What might fossils fail to show?
How are Lamarck’s ideas different from the claim that all evolution happens through local adaptation?
Why should we avoid assuming that every historical theory of species change was an early form of Darwinism?
